en:
You push the gem past the teeth. It rolls up into an eye socket and fits exactly.

Red light spreads through the cracks in the face. The head exhales one slow cloud of dust — and when it clears, a Fire Rune is resting on the stone tongue.

You push the gem past the teeth. It clicks into an eye socket.

A thin bolt skips across the cracked forehead, and the teeth chatter once. The head exhales dust — and a Lightning Rune flickers between its teeth.

You push the gem past the teeth. It settles into an eye socket.

Green light seeps through the cracks, and the mouth curls — almost like remembering pain. The head exhales a bitter cloud. Behind it, a dark green rune rests on the stone tongue.

You set the Crystal Spiderling card down on the cracked floor of the drill room.

The spiderling climbs off the card, taps along the cracks and pulls a grain of crystal out of one.

It climbs back into the picture and keeps the grain.

You slide the card between the stone teeth.

The mouth closes. Stone grinds on stone, and for a few seconds the head chews.

Then the jaw cracks open. A different card is lying on the tongue, damp with gray dust.

You hold the card out to the vines.

They wrap it carefully — almost gently — and sink a few black thorns into its edge.

When they let go, the card is not the same.
A few of them stop chewing when they see what you are carrying. One goblin quietly moves round to your side of the table.
Nobody moves. The thing with too many legs watches both of you and does not pick a side.
The whole room is already laughing. Someone starts collecting bets before you have sat down.

He is stronger than you and both of you know it, so you do not try to out-pull him. You wait until he leans, and then you stop being where he is pushing.

His own weight takes his hand down onto the slab.

The room goes very quiet. The ogre looks at his hand for a while, then at you, and pushes the whole stack of coins across the table without a word.

You get about two seconds of holding him.

Then your knuckles find the stone.

He takes the coins. That is all he takes.

He goes at it properly this time, and it takes everything you have.

When his hand finally goes down the crowd does not cheer. They just look at the ogre.

He unhooks the stone guard and pushes it across to you, then sits back with his arms folded and watches you take it, {card} and all.

He looks at {card} for a long moment, decides it is worth his time, and plants his elbow.

You win by not fighting him where he is strongest.

He pushes his coins over, keeps looking at his own hand, and says something short in Ogrish. The crowd stops laughing. You get the distinct impression this is not finished.

He does not make the same mistake twice.

Your hand is on the slab before you have finished bracing, and {card} goes into the pile beside his elbow.

He buckles the stone guard back onto his forearm and turns away from the table.

He takes {card} off the table before your hand has finished going down.

The crowd is delighted, briefly, and then bored.

You do not say anything. You draw the weapon and rest it against the doors, in the light, where all three of them can see it properly.

The one with the tally board stops writing. The one with the shield finds something interesting on the floor.

Nobody stops you lifting the lid of the strongbox at the foot of the door, and nobody looks at you either. The bar is already off by the time you straighten up.

You press the weapon flat against the glass.

The case opens from the inside. The {magic} settles against the metal and sinks in, and the glass closes over nothing.

The other cases go dark.

What you are holding is called {weapon} now.

You put your elbow through the nearest case.

The glass opens your arm. Whatever was inside is already gone.

You put your elbow through the case holding the {magic}.

The ward goes off late and shallow, opening a line across your forearm — but the card is in your fist and it stays there.

The remaining cases go dark before the glass finishes falling.

You hold the card out over the water. Your reflection lifts the wrong hand.

The card sinks without a sound. A different one comes up, cold and dripping tar.

For a second it feels like you made a deal with yourself.

You put the trinket on the tray. It snaps back into the booth.

The glass goes dark. Then a rainbow sheen spreads across it from the inside — thin and oily, like light on spilled ink.

A card slides out. It is far too bright for the machine that made it.

You put one of your cards on the tray. It snaps back before you can change your mind.

Behind the glass, the wizard looks at the card for a long time. Then it taps the glass twice.

A different card slides out.

The box takes the cog, clicks once, and unfolds a drawer from somewhere no drawer should fit. Then a second. Then a third.

It climbs into your pack and settles in like it has always been there.

Loyal Latchbox: +1 inventory slot

The box swallows the cog. It clicks. It coughs smoke.

Then it plays three flat notes, spits a handful of valuables at your feet, and refuses to look at you.
"Free repair is still repair," the goblin says. "Just shorter."
He chews the card thoughtfully, then bolts half of it into the casing. "Good enough for a machine with low standards."
He counts the coins twice. Then he becomes suddenly, completely professional, which is somehow worse.

The ogre is at the same table. He has not put his coins back out.

Instead he has unbuckled the stone guard from his forearm and laid it on the slab between you. It is scaled, heavy, and clearly not his originally.

The crowd is bigger this time, and much quieter.

{crowd}

An ogre sits at a stone table with one elbow planted on it. Coins are stacked by his hand — more than a goblin toll, less than he seems to think.

A stool waits on your side. It is too small.

Monsters have gathered to watch: a few goblins, something with too many legs, and a skeleton that keeps losing its place in the crowd.

{crowd}

You leave the guard where it is.

The ogre says something in Ogrish that the crowd finds funnier than you do, and buckles it back onto his arm.

He mutters something in Ogrish. The crowd loses interest in you immediately.

The stool stays empty.
(Drag a weapon onto a case.)
(You have no weapon to trade.)

You go along the wall, feeling through the broken cases.

Most hold nothing but glass. One still has something wedged in the corner.
Behind you, {names} keep turning in their cases, waiting for iron that does not come.
You leave the wall alone.
